PolyUMI teaches robots with vision, touch and contact sound

The open-source demonstration platform transfers a sensing finger from a wireless handheld gripper to a robot, supporting slip control and contact-rich tasks.

PolyUMI Research Team ↗24 September 2026English editorial summary
StoryImages 9Videos 6

Recording more than camera images

The PolyUMI team released a preprint on September 24 describing a wireless handheld gripper that synchronizes wrist vision, optical touch, contact audio and motion state. It captures interaction details that an external camera may miss.

Sharing sensing between teaching and execution

The sensing finger transfers from the demonstration gripper to the robot in about ten minutes, preserving sensing geometry. Its reported parts cost is roughly $236; that is not the price of a complete robot or collection system.

Combining signals with VisTA

VisTA combines observations across sensors and time to generate actions. In a task that lets a screwdriver rotate downward before catching it, vision, touch and audio succeeded in eight of ten trials, versus two of ten with vision alone.

Limits of the evidence

Extra sensors did not improve every task. All compared methods reached at least 80% on lightbulb turning, and the slip-control comparison used only ten trials per configuration. The results do not establish long-term industrial reliability. The project provides code, explanatory figures and experiment videos for inspection.
